label: PART I
title: Reasoning About Design
lead: Learn the forces behind the catalog before memorizing its names.

chapters.title: The mental model
chapters.intro: Before learning a catalog of names, learn the forces behind them. These concepts explain why a change makes code easier or harder to live with.

concepts.title: Refactoring
concepts.definition: Refactoring is a controlled change to code's internal organization that leaves its observable behavior intact. Its purpose is to make later changes easier, safer, or clearer.
concepts.look_for: Use it when working code hides intent, duplicates knowledge, tangles responsibilities, or makes the next requirement risky. Establish a fast behavioral check before changing the structure.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before: the price calculation is embedded in the caller.
total = 0
for line in order.lines:
    total += line.unit_price * line.quantity

# After: the same calculation has a name and one owner.
def calculate_total(order):
    total = 0
    for line in order.lines:
        total += line.unit_price * line.quantity
    return total


refactored_total = calculate_total(order)
concepts.python_shorthand:
def calculate_total(order):
    return sum(line.unit_price * line.quantity for line in order.lines)
concepts.walkthrough: Before the change, the caller knows how an order total is assembled: it iterates through `order.Lines` and multiplies each `UnitPrice` by `Quantity`. After Extract Method, `CalculateTotal` owns that calculation and the caller asks for the result. The arithmetic and resulting value do not change; only the location and name of the behavior change. That unchanged result is what makes this a refactoring rather than a feature change. The new method gives the calculation a stable home, so a future pricing adjustment can be made in one place and tested directly. The Python version performs the same move into `calculate_total`. The shorthand variants show common collection expressions, but the loops make the preserved behavior easiest to compare. Extract Method is the particular refactoring used here; refactoring is the broader discipline of making such behavior-preserving structural changes in small, verifiable steps.
concepts.caution: Do not use 'refactoring' as a synonym for a rewrite, cleanup campaign, or feature change. Separate behavior changes whenever practical so failures have a small search area.
concepts.related: Related: Behavior-preserving change; Extract Method; Characterization Test

concepts.title: Behavior-preserving change
concepts.definition: Behavior-preserving change is the safety condition behind refactoring: outcomes that matter to callers remain the same even though the implementation is reorganized.
concepts.look_for: Identify the observable contract before editing risky code. Protect representative outputs, exceptions, side effects, and boundary interactions, then change one structural element at a time.
concepts.python_expanded:
def price_after_discount(price, rate):
    discount_amount = price * rate
    final_price = price - discount_amount
    return final_price


def test_refactoring_keeps_the_discounted_price():
    result = price_after_discount(100, 0.10)
    assert result == 90
concepts.walkthrough: The test names one observable promise: supplying `100` and `0.10` to `PriceAfterDiscount` produces `90`. Inside the method, the calculation is deliberately written with `discountAmount` and `finalPrice`; those locals can later be renamed, extracted, inlined, or rearranged while the assertion continues to protect the result. The test does not demand a particular implementation. It cares about what a caller can observe. The Python test gives `price_after_discount` the same boundary. In production code, observable behavior can include more than a return value: which exception is raised, whether a record is saved, or which message is published may also be part of the contract. Compiler checks and static analysis can protect type-level facts, while tests protect selected runtime facts. None of them proves that every behavior is unchanged, but small steps plus focused checks make the claim credible enough to work safely.
concepts.caution: A green test suite protects only what it observes. Around poorly understood legacy code, add characterization tests before assuming an untested edge case is expendable.
concepts.related: Related: Refactoring; Characterization Test; Regression Test

concepts.title: Code smell
concepts.definition: A code smell is a visible clue that a design may make some likely change difficult. It prompts investigation; it is not proof that the code is defective.
concepts.look_for: When a construct feels awkward, name the concrete pressure: which change, test, or debugging task is expensive because of it? Refactor only when that cost matters.
concepts.walkthrough: The original conditional is not automatically bad. It becomes a smell when the shipping eligibility rule is hard to recognize, repeated, or likely to gain another clause. Naming that rule `CanShip` or `can_ship` creates a place where readers can ask what makes an order shippable and where a future rule change can be made once. The smell is therefore not 'a condition exists.' The diagnostic question is whether the condition hides business knowledge and makes the next change costly. Extracting the method is one possible response, not part of the definition of a smell. If the rule is used only once, remains stable, and is already obvious to the team, leaving it inline may be the better choice. This distinction matters in reviews: saying 'this is a code smell' should begin a conversation about change pressure, not end one with a catalog-based verdict.
concepts.caution: Do not refactor merely to make a catalog entry disappear. Churn, defect risk, expected change, and the team's ability to read the current form all matter.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Method; Duplicate Code; Speculative Generality

concepts.title: Design pattern
concepts.definition: A design pattern is a named arrangement of collaborating responsibilities that repeatedly solves a design problem. The name is useful only when the problem, participants, and trade-offs are understood.
concepts.look_for: Reach for a pattern after identifying a recurring variation or coordination problem. Prefer the smallest implementation that makes the participating roles and the expected change explicit.
concepts.walkthrough: This example uses Strategy to make the general idea of a design pattern concrete. `TotalCalculator` owns the stable workflow: add the prices, then apply a discount. `IDiscountStrategy` names the behavior that varies. `NoDiscount` and `HolidayDiscount` provide two interchangeable implementations, and the client selects one without changing `Calculate`. Those participant roles - context, strategy contract, and concrete strategies - are what earn the design its pattern name. The C# shorthand uses a `Func<decimal, decimal>` delegate instead of an interface. The statement lambda and expression lambda are language mechanisms for supplying the same varying behavior; they do not create a different design problem. Python relies on its ordinary callable protocol rather than a declared interface. This is also dependency injection because the client supplies the discount, but Strategy names the role the injected object or function plays. The trade-off is another abstraction to understand, so a single stable discount rule would not justify this machinery.
concepts.caution: A pattern is not evidence of sophistication. If a direct method or small conditional solves a stable problem more clearly, use it.
concepts.related: Related: Strategy; Dependency injection; Higher-order function

concepts.title: Cohesion and coupling
concepts.definition: Cohesion measures how strongly the responsibilities inside a module belong together. Coupling measures how much one part must know about another. Good boundaries usually strengthen cohesion and remove unnecessary coupling.
concepts.look_for: Suspect low cohesion when one class changes for unrelated business reasons. Suspect excessive coupling when a small implementation change forces coordinated edits in many consumers.
concepts.walkthrough: `InvoiceCalculator` groups only arithmetic over invoice lines, so a pricing-rule change has one focused destination. `InvoiceMailer` owns delivery and depends only on `IEmailSender`. SMTP configuration can change without disturbing the calculation, and a tax change does not require reopening email code. That is higher cohesion: each class contains behavior serving one recognizable purpose. It also reduces unnecessary coupling because the calculator knows nothing about email and the mailer knows nothing about how totals are assembled. The two classes may still collaborate in a checkout workflow; coupling itself is not a defect. The goal is for dependencies to be explicit and aligned with stable responsibilities. Merely splitting a large class into two files would not help if both still reached into each other's fields or changed together for every requirement. The Python version expresses the same boundaries without a declared interface, relying on the `email_sender` object's supported behavior.
concepts.caution: Zero coupling is neither possible nor desirable. Prefer a few explicit dependencies with stable contracts over many layers of forwarding that only hide the same dependency graph.
concepts.related: Related: Single Responsibility Principle; Encapsulation; Dependency Inversion Principle

concepts.title: Encapsulation and information hiding
concepts.definition: Encapsulation lets a type control valid state transitions. Information hiding keeps volatile implementation decisions behind a stable public surface; public fields with ceremonial accessors provide neither benefit by themselves.
concepts.look_for: Use a behavior-bearing method when callers should request a valid transition, not retrieve data and assemble the transition themselves.
concepts.walkthrough: `Account` does not expose a public setter for `Balance`. A caller can observe the balance, but the only shown transition is `Deposit`, which rejects zero and negative amounts before changing the private `balance` field. That is encapsulation: the object keeps its invariant true by owning the mutation. Information hiding is the related boundary benefit. Callers depend on `Deposit` and `Balance`, not on whether the amount is stored in one field, reconstructed from transactions, or loaded lazily. The implementation may change without requiring callers to change. Python's underscore in `_balance` is a convention rather than access enforcement, but `deposit` still creates the behavioral boundary. The point is not that every field must be private. An immutable coordinate can be transparent because no invalid transition is possible. Encapsulation earns its cost when state has rules, a lifecycle, or an implementation decision that consumers should not own.
concepts.caution: Do not hide simple immutable data behind boilerplate solely to appear object-oriented. Encapsulate where a type must protect a rule or preserve freedom to change an implementation.
concepts.related: Related: Information hiding; Tell, Don't Ask; Anemic Domain Model

concepts.title: Abstraction and indirection
concepts.definition: An abstraction names the capability a caller needs. Indirection places a boundary between that caller and a concrete implementation so selected variation, cost, or external behavior can be isolated.
concepts.look_for: Introduce a boundary when a dependency is external, volatile, slow, nondeterministic, or needs a controlled substitute in tests. Remove it when it only adds navigation.
concepts.walkthrough: `TokenPolicy` needs current time, not knowledge of the operating system clock. `IClock` expresses that narrower capability. The injected `clock` adds indirection: `IsExpired` reaches time through a collaborator instead of calling `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` directly. That extra hop earns its place because time is nondeterministic and tests can supply a fixed clock. It also confines a platform decision behind one interface. Abstraction and indirection are related but distinct. `IClock` is the abstraction - the vocabulary of the needed capability. Holding an `IClock` between `TokenPolicy` and the system clock is the indirection. A useful boundary absorbs change or controls an effect; an interface copied mechanically from a concrete library may simply relocate complexity. Python's `Clock` protocol documents the expected operation and supports static checking, although ordinary duck typing could provide the same runtime substitution.
concepts.caution: An interface with one implementation can still be justified by a real boundary, but do not create interfaces reflexively. Each level should buy isolation, clarity, policy ownership, or test control.
concepts.related: Related: Dependency Inversion Principle; Dependency injection; Test Double

concepts.title: DRY: one source of truth
concepts.definition: DRY means that one piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation. It targets duplicated rules and decisions, not every pair of similar-looking lines.
concepts.look_for: Consolidate copies when they must change together for the same reason. Leave them separate when their similarity is accidental or their future rules can diverge.
concepts.walkthrough: Both callers need the same policy: adulthood begins on the customer's eighteenth birthday. `EligibilityRules.IsAdult` gives that policy one implementation, so a correction to date handling reaches account opening and contract signing together. The important duplication would be the age rule, not the fact that both callers contain an `if` statement or happen to use similar variable names. This is why DRY is better understood as one source of truth than as 'never repeat code.' If the legal age for contracts later differs from the age for opening an account, the two callers no longer share one piece of knowledge and should receive separately named policies. The Python sample calculates completed years explicitly. Leap-day treatment can be jurisdiction-specific, which is precisely the kind of policy detail that benefits from one authoritative owner.
concepts.caution: Prematurely merging coincidental similarity creates an abstraction that unrelated callers must fight. Wait until the shared knowledge and reason for change are clear.
concepts.related: Related: Duplicate Code; Shotgun Surgery; Single source of truth

concepts.title: KISS: keep the design direct
concepts.definition: KISS favors the most direct design that clearly satisfies known requirements. Simplicity concerns how easily behavior can be predicted and changed, not how few characters are typed.
concepts.look_for: Prefer ordinary control flow and familiar data structures while the cases are few and stable. Introduce a larger mechanism only when actual variation makes the direct form costly.
concepts.walkthrough: `GetStatusLabel` has a closed, local decision with two known cases. Straightforward branches make the mapping visible without introducing a strategy registry, polymorphic hierarchy, or configurable pipeline. A reader can predict the fallback and add a third case in one place. That directness is the KISS benefit. The C# switch-expression alternative is shorter and equally clear once the syntax is familiar; it does not make the design more sophisticated. Python's dictionary form is compact, but the explicit `if` statements make control flow and the default obvious. KISS does not command teams to avoid abstractions. If status-specific behavior spreads across many operations, polymorphism may eventually become simpler than repeated branching. Nor does KISS justify omitting validation or error handling. The relevant question is which design carries the lowest mental and change cost for the requirements and risks that actually exist.
concepts.caution: Do not use 'keep it simple' to defend missing correctness, security, or failure handling. Thorough code can still be direct and predictable.
concepts.related: Related: YAGNI; Speculative Generality; Switch Statements

concepts.title: YAGNI: build for evidence, not imagination
concepts.definition: YAGNI - You Aren't Gonna Need It - warns against paying now for flexibility supported only by imagined requirements. Implement today's need cleanly and add variation when evidence appears.
concepts.look_for: Remove unused extension points, configuration switches, generic frameworks, and alternate implementations that have no current caller or committed requirement.
concepts.walkthrough: The requirement says to email one receipt, so `ReceiptService.SendReceiptAsync` renders it and asks `IEmailSender` to send it. The code does not invent a plug-in pipeline for SMS, push notifications, fax, scheduled delivery, or user-selectable templates. Those capabilities can be added when a real scenario requires them. The email boundary is still explicit because an external delivery system is a credible source of volatility and test difficulty; YAGNI does not require hard-coding every dependency. The distinction is between a cheap, justified seam and a speculative framework. Python follows the same direct workflow through `send_receipt`. A future second channel might justify a notification strategy, but adding that strategy today would make every reader understand variation that no caller uses. Keeping the method cohesive and the dependency visible leaves the code ready to refactor when evidence arrives without prepaying for a guessed design.
concepts.caution: YAGNI does not excuse choices that are expensive or impossible to reverse. Preserve simple seams around high-risk external systems, data formats, and security boundaries.
concepts.related: Related: KISS; Speculative Generality; Open/Closed Principle

concepts.title: Single Responsibility Principle
concepts.definition: The Single Responsibility Principle says a module should answer to one coherent source of change, usually one business capability or actor. It does not require one method per class.
concepts.look_for: Split a module when unrelated policies repeatedly change independently inside it, especially when different stakeholders request those changes.
concepts.walkthrough: Pricing rules live in `InvoiceCalculator.CalculateTotal`; delivery behavior lives in `InvoiceEmailer.SendAsync`. A change requested by finance - for example, a new surcharge - affects the calculator. A change requested by communications or infrastructure - for example, a new email provider - affects the emailer. Keeping those policies apart gives each class one coherent reason to change. The classes can contain multiple methods as long as those methods serve the same responsibility. Conversely, a one-method class can still violate SRP if that method mixes pricing, persistence, and delivery. The Python classes establish the same ownership without formal interfaces. This example also has high cohesion, but the terms emphasize different things: cohesion describes how well the contents belong together; SRP asks whether independent change forces have been placed in the same module. An application service may coordinate both collaborators without inheriting either responsibility.
concepts.caution: Splitting every operation into a separate class creates indirection without autonomy. Keep behavior together when it changes for the same reason and speaks the same domain vocabulary.
concepts.related: Related: Cohesion and coupling; Extract Class; Divergent Change

concepts.title: Open/Closed Principle
concepts.definition: The Open/Closed Principle asks stable policy to accept new behavior through a deliberate extension point instead of being edited for every new case. Apply it to a demonstrated axis of variation.
concepts.look_for: Use a strategy, callback, or implementation boundary when new cases arrive repeatedly and the coordinating workflow should remain stable.
concepts.walkthrough: `Checkout.CalculateTotal` contains the stable workflow: accept a subtotal and apply a selected policy. `IDiscountPolicy` marks discount calculation as the variation point. Adding `EmployeeDiscount` would require a new implementation but would not require another branch inside `Checkout`. In that specific sense, checkout is closed to repeated modification and open to additional discount behavior. Existing classes are never literally closed - defects and genuinely new requirements can still require edits. The principle is about designing a known axis of variation so routine additions do not destabilize the coordinator. Python achieves the same substitution through compatible `apply` methods rather than a declared interface. This arrangement is also the Strategy pattern; Open/Closed names the design goal, while Strategy names one structure used to achieve it. If discount rules are stable or only two simple cases exist, a conditional may remain clearer than the extra types.
concepts.caution: Do not build an extension framework around every conditional. The abstraction is justified when the variation is real, recurring, and important enough to keep the caller stable.
concepts.related: Related: Strategy; Dependency Inversion Principle; Speculative Generality

concepts.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
concepts.definition: The Liskov Substitution Principle requires every subtype to honor the behavioral promises of its base type: valid inputs, results, invariants, and meaningful side effects.
concepts.look_for: Investigate overrides that throw 'not supported,' demand stricter preconditions, weaken guarantees, or force callers to identify the concrete subtype before using it.
concepts.walkthrough: A read-only file can honestly satisfy `IReadableFile`: every client that receives that interface may call `ReadAllText` and get the promised behavior. It does not pretend to implement `IWritableFile` and then throw from `WriteAllText`. `EditableFile` supports the stronger contract because it can both read and write. A function such as Python's `print_contents` depends only on reading, so any object honoring that protocol can be substituted without a type check or special case. LSP is therefore not mainly about inheritance syntax. It is about semantic substitutability. A subtype violates the principle when it accepts the base type's name but rejects valid base inputs, returns incompatible meaning, or changes required side effects. Splitting capabilities into honest interfaces also supports Interface Segregation, but the emphasis differs: ISP protects clients from unused dependencies; LSP protects the behavioral truth of substitution.
concepts.caution: Inheritance used only to reuse implementation can create a false subtype. Prefer composition or a narrower contract when the supposed child cannot honor the parent's meaning.
concepts.related: Related: Interface Segregation Principle; Refused Bequest; Design by Contract

concepts.title: Interface Segregation Principle
concepts.definition: The Interface Segregation Principle says clients should depend on focused capabilities they actually use, and implementations should not be forced to promise irrelevant operations.
concepts.look_for: Split a broad interface when consumers require different permissions or implementers leave methods empty, throw from them, or depend on resources they should not need.
concepts.walkthrough: `OrderViewer` can only read orders because its constructor accepts `IOrderReader`. It neither knows about nor receives the `Save` operation. A read-only implementation can therefore satisfy the contract honestly, and the viewer can be given credentials that cannot write. Code that updates orders can separately depend on `IOrderWriter`. This separation follows actual client roles rather than an arbitrary one-method rule. If most consumers always need both operations, a combined repository interface may be more coherent. Python protocols provide the same role-focused documentation and static checking while runtime compatibility remains structural. The example also supports least privilege, but ISP is primarily a dependency-design principle: a change to writing should not force read-only clients to recompile, retest, or provide dummy behavior. Interface Segregation and Liskov Substitution often reinforce each other because narrower interfaces make honest substitution easier.
concepts.caution: Do not create a microscopic interface for every method. Split contracts along real consumer roles, permissions, ownership, and change boundaries.
concepts.related: Related: Liskov Substitution Principle; Least privilege; Role Interface

concepts.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
concepts.definition: The Dependency Inversion Principle places high-level policy and low-level details behind an abstraction shaped by the policy's needs. Source dependencies point toward the stable business rule.
concepts.look_for: Introduce a policy-owned port when business logic directly imports a database, file system, clock, HTTP client, message broker, or framework-specific API.
concepts.walkthrough: `CheckoutService` contains the high-level policy: complete an order and persist the result. It depends on `IOrderStore`, a contract stated in application vocabulary, rather than on SQL commands or a database SDK. `SqlOrderStore` lives on the detail side and implements that contract, so its source dependency points toward the policy-owned abstraction. A file-backed or in-memory store can do the same. Passing `store` through the constructor is dependency injection; making checkout depend on the abstraction rather than the SQL class is dependency inversion. Those terms are related but not interchangeable. Python's `OrderStore` protocol makes the same expected capability explicit without requiring nominal inheritance. The boundary protects checkout from database churn and lets tests use a small in-memory implementation. It should expose what checkout needs - `Save` - rather than mirror an entire vendor client and leak detail operations upward.
concepts.caution: Do not create an abstraction that merely reproduces every method of a low-level library. The port should speak the policy's language and remain narrower than the detail it hides.
concepts.related: Related: Dependency injection; Ports and Adapters; Abstraction and indirection

concepts.title: Composition over inheritance
concepts.definition: Composition builds behavior by giving an object collaborators. Inheritance acquires behavior by joining a subtype contract. Prefer composition when capabilities vary independently or the relationship is 'has' rather than a durable 'is.'
concepts.look_for: Choose composition when a subclass would inherit irrelevant operations, several dimensions vary independently, or behavior must be selected at runtime.
concepts.walkthrough: `ReportExporter` has an `IReportFormatter`; it is not a special kind of formatter. `Export` delegates the representation decision to that collaborator. A JSON formatter can be supplied without creating `JsonReportExporter`, and other exporter behavior can evolve without duplicating a class hierarchy for every format. Composition therefore isolates the varying capability and allows runtime assembly. Inheritance would be appropriate if a subtype genuinely promised all semantics of its base and the taxonomy itself mattered. The preference for composition is aimed at avoiding fragile base classes and combinatorial subclass trees, not banning inheritance. Python uses the same object composition through its `formatter` field, relying on compatible behavior rather than a declared interface. The example also resembles Strategy because formatting is interchangeable, but 'composition over inheritance' describes the construction choice, while Strategy describes the collaborator's design role.
concepts.caution: Inheritance remains useful for honest substitutable taxonomies and framework extension points. Replace it only when composition produces a clearer ownership model or avoids a false 'is-a' claim.
concepts.related: Related: Strategy; Liskov Substitution Principle; Replace Inheritance with Delegation

concepts.title: Dependency injection
concepts.definition: Dependency injection supplies an object's collaborators from outside rather than having the object construct or locate them. Required dependencies become visible, replaceable, and testable.
concepts.look_for: Prefer constructor injection for required long-lived collaborators. Use method injection when a dependency genuinely belongs to one operation or request scope.
concepts.walkthrough: `ReceiptService` declares `IEmailSender` in its constructor and stores the supplied collaborator. The composition code creates `SmtpEmailSender` and injects it into the service. Receipt behavior no longer decides how to construct SMTP infrastructure, and a test can supply a recording sender. Constructor injection also makes an invalid service harder to create because the required dependency is visible at construction. The C# shorthand uses a primary constructor and expression-bodied method; it compresses the same dependency graph and does not change the technique. Python performs injection by ordinary constructor assignment. A dependency-injection container may automate the outer wiring, but the pattern does not require one. DI describes how a dependency is supplied. Dependency Inversion separately asks what direction the source-level abstraction points, and Strategy may describe the role an injected collaborator plays. Keeping those names separate makes architecture discussions far more precise.
concepts.caution: A service locator hides dependencies behind ambient access and is not equivalent to injection. Keep container use near the composition root rather than resolving services throughout business code.
concepts.related: Related: Dependency Inversion Principle; Composition Root; Service Locator

concepts.title: Immutability
concepts.definition: An immutable value cannot change after it is created. New states are represented by new values, reducing hidden mutation history and making sharing and concurrency easier to reason about.
concepts.look_for: Favor immutability for value objects, configuration, messages, and results. Isolate mutation behind one owner when updates are necessary.
concepts.walkthrough: `Money.Add` never changes `Amount` on the existing object. It verifies that currencies match, computes `combinedAmount`, and returns a new `Money`. Any code holding either original value can rely on it remaining unchanged, which removes a large class of aliasing surprises. The C# record shorthand expresses value-oriented equality and uses `with` to create a modified copy; the expanded class makes the construction and invariant check explicit. Python's frozen dataclass prevents ordinary field reassignment and follows the same return-a-new-value model. Immutability is especially useful for messages passed between threads or components because no recipient can change what another recipient sees. It is not the same as purity: `Add` is pure here, but an immutable object could still call external services. Nor does it eliminate all mutation; collections, caches, and high-volume algorithms may need controlled internal updates.
concepts.caution: Copying large immutable structures can consume time and memory. Use persistent collections, builders, or tightly owned mutation when measurement shows a real cost.
concepts.related: Related: Value Object; Mutable Shared State; Pure Function

concepts.title: Functional core, imperative shell
concepts.definition: Functional core, imperative shell separates deterministic decisions from effects. Pure calculations live in the core; a thin shell performs I/O, reads time, handles failures, and coordinates the world.
concepts.look_for: Separate business calculation from database, HTTP, file, UI, logging, clock, and randomness work when mixed effects make tests or failure handling difficult.
concepts.python_expanded:
def calculate_total(lines):
    total = 0
    for line in lines:
        total += line.unit_price * line.quantity
    return total


async def checkout(order_id, order_store):
    order = await order_store.load(order_id)
    total = calculate_total(order.lines)
    await order_store.save_total(order_id, total)
concepts.walkthrough: `CalculateTotal` is the functional core. Given the same line values, it returns the same total and performs no I/O. `CheckoutAsync` is the imperative shell: it loads an order, passes plain data into the calculation, and saves the result. Tests can exercise pricing with ordinary values, while a smaller set of integration tests covers the store and async coordination. Failure handling also has an honest location because loading and saving remain visible in the shell. The shorthand C# version uses LINQ to express the pure aggregation; the architectural split is unchanged. Python follows the same division. This style does not eliminate side effects or imply that every method must be pure. It concentrates effects at boundaries where timeouts, retries, transactions, cancellation, and logging can be handled deliberately. It differs from layered architecture in scale: functional core/imperative shell can guide a single operation even inside a larger architecture.
concepts.caution: Do not hide side effects inside functions merely labeled as core. Purity is a behavioral property, and the shell still needs deliberate failure and consistency policies.
concepts.related: Related: Pure Function; Command-query separation; Hexagonal Architecture

concepts.title: Command-query separation
concepts.definition: Command-query separation distinguishes operations that observe state from operations that change it. A query should not produce surprising state changes; a command should make its mutation clear.
concepts.look_for: Split methods whose names, return values, or hidden side effects make callers unsure whether invoking them changes anything.
concepts.walkthrough: `GetBalance` is a query: it returns information and leaves `balance` unchanged. `Withdraw` is a command: its name announces a state transition, it validates the request, and then subtracts from `balance`. A caller can therefore reason about whether a line is observational or mutating without reading the implementation. The principle discourages a method such as `GetBalanceAndApplyFees`, whose return value disguises a write. Python expresses the same distinction by convention rather than through the type system. Command-query separation is a design guideline, not an absolute ban on returning information from mutations. Atomic operations such as `TryDequeue`, database `INSERT ... RETURNING`, or a command returning a newly assigned identifier legitimately combine a change with a result because separating them would introduce races or extra work. In those cases, name the dual behavior plainly and document the contract.
concepts.caution: Do not split an inherently atomic change-and-return operation into separate calls. Preserve atomicity and make the combined semantics explicit in the name and result type.
concepts.related: Related: Command Query Responsibility Segregation; Tell, Don't Ask; Idempotency
